Expected.why: ctx is a parameter but never used; context.Background() is passed to both NewRequestWithContext and getTextCapped, so the caller's timeout and cancellation cannot stop the request or the body read. Bitbucket has no Client.Timeout by design, which makes the caller's ctx the only bound on a 10 MiB diff.
The Unlock now runs only on the success path, so returning the unknown-team error leaves r.mu locked and every subsequent caller blocks forever.

Findings.Comment: The change removes the early return when `r.Ticket` is nil but falls through to the return statement that unconditionally accesses `r.Ticket.Key`. This will cause a nil pointer dereference panic when `Summarize` is called with a `Result` whose `Ticket` is nil. The original code correctly returned just `r.Body` in that case; the new code must preserve that behavior.
Findings.Headline: Nil pointer dereference when Ticket is nil — blocking bug

Expected.why: The nil branch no longer returns, so r.Ticket.Key panics whenever Ticket is nil. A reviewer may anchor on the dead check (19) or on the dereference (22).

Findings.Comment: The boundary condition change in `ContextAfter` causes an off-by-one error that will panic at runtime. When `first` is less than `len(lines)` and `first + n` equals exactly `len(lines)`, the condition `last >= len(lines)` now sets `last = len(lines) + 1`. Slicing `lines[first:last]` with `last` exceeding the slice length will cause an index out of range panic. The original guard `last > len(lines)` setting `last = len(lines)` correctly prevents this.
Findings.Headline: Off-by-one error will cause slice bounds out of range panic

Expected.why: The clamp sets last to len(lines)+1, so the final slice expression lines[first:last] runs one past the length. With no spare capacity that panics; with spare capacity it silently yields a phantom trailing line, which is the quieter half of the bug.

Findings.Comment: Removing `defer resp.Body.Close()` leaks the HTTP response body on every call. In Go, `resp.Body` from `http.Client.Do()` must be closed to release the underlying TCP connection back to the pool. Without this, each call to `WhoAmI` ties up a connection permanently, leading to connection pool exhaustion under sustained load — eventually causing blocking or failures on subsequent HTTP calls.
Findings.Headline: Remove defer resp.Body.Close leaks connections — blocking

Expected.why: The response body is never closed on any path, so the underlying connection is leaked on every call, successful or not.

Findings.Comment: Removing the mutex lock around the `q.depth` assignment in the `worker` goroutine introduces a data race. `q.depth` is written here without synchronization while `Submit` and `Depth` read/write it under the mutex. For example, if a `Submit` call runs concurrently with this line, both may write to `q.depth` simultaneously, violating Go's memory model and potentially corrupting the value.
Findings.Headline: Data race on q.depth in worker loop — fix required

Expected.why: The worker goroutine writes q.depth and reads q.pending without holding q.mu, while Submit writes and Depth reads the same fields under the mutex; that is a data race.

Findings.Comment: The diff removes error handling from `tx.Commit(ctx)`. If the commit fails (due to network issues, database constraints, etc.), the function returns `nil` despite the transaction being rolled back by the deferred `tx.Rollback(ctx)`. The caller will believe the claim was successfully added when it was not, leading to silent data loss or inconsistent state.
Findings.Headline: Ignored error from tx.Commit can lead to silent data loss

Expected.why: tx.Commit's error is discarded, so a failed commit is reported to the caller as success and the claim silently does not exist.

Findings.Comment: The two error conditions are swapped. When the project has no claim (no rows), the function now returns an error wrapping `errNoRows` instead of `ErrNoClaim`, and when there is a database fault, it returns an error wrapping `ErrNoClaim` instead of the original error. This breaks the contract that callers can use `errors.Is(err, ErrNoClaim)` to check for no claim and will misrepresent database faults as no-claim. The second condition at line 22 must also be changed to `return "", fmt.Errorf("owner of %q: %w", project, err)`.
Findings.Headline: Error returns are swapped in Store.Owner — incorrect error wrapping for no-claim vs database fault

Expected.why: The branches wrap each other's error: errors.Is(err, ErrNoClaim) is now false when the project is genuinely unclaimed and true when the query failed, so a database fault is treated as an unowned project.
